In this paper, we explore whether diffusion models can generate the parameters of policy networks in reinforcement learning (RL), and whether the generated policies exhibit generalization capabilities. To achieve this, we propose Diffusion-based Conditional Policy Network Parameter Generation (DPPG), which consists of a Transformer-based autoencoder and a task-conditioned diffusion model. The autoencoder achieves a high compression rate by patchifying network parameters, while the task-conditioned diffusion model generates corresponding parameters conditioned on different environments. Our experiments demonstrate that, with a single unified DPPG model, we can synthesize high-quality policies across a diverse set of tasks from different environment domains, including Classic Control, Atari games, and MuJoCo. Additionally, our method can generate networks with a larger number of parameters compared to previous approaches. Furthermore, we find that in previously unseen environments, DPPG can generate parameters that achieve faster convergence and reach competitive performance, showcasing the potential future applications of parameter generation via diffusion.
  </details>

- **[Ground-Wing: A Parametric 3D Wing-in-Ground-Effect Dataset for Benchmarking Neural Surrogate Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04571)**  `arXiv:2611.04571`  
  _Andrea Cenzato, Lukas Karch, Andre Luckow, Yoran Pichon, Francesco Pasqua, Abouzar Ghasemi, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  This paper presents a CFD dataset of a highly parametrized 3D wing operating in ground effect, designed for benchmarking neural surrogate models for aerodynamic prediction, using a wing shape and flow conditions typically encountered in motorsport applications. The dataset comprises 770 RANS simulations of 194 unique wing configurations, sampled across 27 airfoil profile variants and 4 distances from the ground, spanning variations in wing sweep, chord, taper, angle of attack, and tip twist. Six neural network architectures representing distinct paradigms --- convolutional (DoMINO), graph-based (X-MeshGraphNet), transformer-based (AB-UPT, GeoTransolver, GAOT), and JEPA-based (AeroJEPA) --- are evaluated on their ability to predict surface pressure coefficient and wall shear stress distributions, from which integral drag and lift coefficients are recovered. The dataset is intended to be used as a challenging benchmark for surrogate CFD models, due to the uniqueness of the ground effect being absent from other wing and airfoil datasets. The dataset is available for download atthis https URL
  </details>

- **[A Hybrid Visitor Prediction Framework using Interpretable Temporal features, Integrating IQR and Anomaly Detection in Lakes in Nebraska](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03486)**  `arXiv:2611.03486`  
  _Israt Zarin, Christopher Chizinski_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  For effective resource management, infrastructure planning, and sustainable tourism, it is really important to predict accurate visitors. This paper estimates the daily visitation of Nebraska lakes using spatial, basic temporal, and interpretable temporal features. Moreover, we evaluate the base models with multiple metrics. Using the best three models, our method will ensemble hybrid models and choose the best hybrid technique. Further, we investigate the impact of lag features and how the models work with different outlier detection techniques such as Interquartile Range (IQR) and anomaly detection. The models are evaluated using regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE, and R2). Experiment results show that, after removing anomalies, MAE, MSE, RMSE, and MAPE are reduced. Adding lag features also shows some positive effects on the results. Moreover, anomaly detection techniques perform better than IQR in improving performance while preserving data. The reported anomaly-based cross-validation results favored the voting ensemble over the compared base models on the evaluated metrics. In anomaly-based cross-validation, VOTE improved prediction errors compared with MLP (256,128,64); improvements varied in the single-split comparison. Specifically, the hybrid model reduced MAE by 9.82%, MSE by 3.12%, RMSE by 1.76%, and MAPE by 6.77%. In the reported cross-validation comparison, the best anomaly-based hybrid model had lower MAE, MSE, RMSE, and MAPE than the best IQR-based hybrid model by 9.81%, 34.30%, 18.99%, and 0.66%, respectively.
  </details>

- **[ReFrame: Silence-Aware Compute Reclamation for Full-Duplex Speech Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01835)**  `arXiv:2611.01835`  
  _Zheng Zhou, Guanyi Chen, Jing Wei, Haoyuan Liang, Jian Zhang, Haohuan Fu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Full-duplex speech models execute dense model inference for every audio frame throughout a live interaction. This uniform framewise schedule creates sustained GPU load across dialogue states whose computation has strong, reusable temporal structure. ReFrame formulates full-duplex inference as a silence-aware computation problem. Mutual Silence Speculation (MSS) operates when both participants are silent: it evaluates multi-frame Temporal continuations, verifies text and hidden-state stability, and applies batched Mimi audio-token correction. Listening Frame Folding (LFF) operates while the user speaks and the agent listens: it processes already-arrived user frames through parallel Temporal execution and frame-batched audio-token generation while accepting only the verified prefix. Frame-Budget Reinvestment (FBR) assigns the released frame intervals to resumable external retrieval and language-model workers, then injects timely references through Moshi's conditioning interface. We instantiate ReFrame on five full-duplex models spanning Moshi-family, phase-structured, and flattened autoregressive generation. Across the complete 1,225-conversation FDBench, ReFrame reduces measured GPU execution time by 18.80-31.01% and retains 96.92-100% non-PAD text agreement on five different models. On HaluEval tests, FBR increases the number of correct generated spoken answers from 86 to 205 under the same auxiliary-service budget. ReFrame turns recurring dialogue structure into lower inference cost and higher end-to-end service capability.
  </details>

- **[Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01472)**  `arXiv:2611.01472`  
  _Ming Lian_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Causal masking obstructs the column balancing used by optimal-transport (OT) attention. We study an unbalanced OT operator that uses only current and earlier rows and characterize its induced positional prior. For bounded scores and any fixed balancing strength below one, its fixed point assigns vanishing mass to every fixed window as context grows. With constant scores, the prior has an exact scale-invariant form. We classify positional encodings by whether they prevent this dilution. We also derive finite-length window-mass bounds for log-distance priors with exponents near one. Preregistered experiments use 25M- and 100M-parameter language models. The OT operator improves loss extrapolation over softmax, while exploratory comparisons favor an explicit distance bias at a fraction of the cost. Changing only the bias beyond the training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints. During training, learned exponents approach one even when constrained above it. A margin chosen from prior calculations controls distant-mass growth in the tested setting.
  </details>

- **[MXCode: Vector Quantization for MX-Native Inference at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00403)**  `arXiv:2611.00403`  
  _Gaurav Kolhe, Cansu Demirkiran, Shubhi Tyagi, Sulaiman Sadiq, Boyao Wang, Richard Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Memory capacity and bandwidth are major bottlenecks in LLM inference, motivating weight compression beyond conventional 4-bit quantization. Vector quantization (VQ) enables approximately 2-bit weight storage but often relies on codebooks incompatible with native FP4 computation. We introduce MXCode (MX-Native Codebook Quantization), a framework bridging ultra-low-bit VQ compression with MicroXcaling (MX)-native FP4 computation. MXCode proposes three strategies: PostScale, which quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4; PreScale, which extracts MX scales before codebook learning; and PreScale+, which further compresses these scales using VQ. These strategies explore tradeoffs among quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity. All reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands without materializing intermediate high-precision weights. We evaluate MXCode on Qwen3 (235B), DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and GLM-5.2 (753B) using the Microsoft MX Emulation Library. MXCode achieves approximately 2 bits per weight with competitive, workload-dependent model quality. On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.
  </details>

- **[OCELOT: Planetary-Scale Species Distribution Modeling with Satellite Foundation Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00284)**  `arXiv:2611.00284`  
  _Bart van Merriënboer, Lauren Harrell, Keith Anderson, Burcu Karagol Ayan, Elise Kleeman, Tom Denton, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Large-scale repositories of species observations now contain billions of occurrence records from around the world, but these sightings cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use only a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated on extrapolating to remote, unvisited regions--where species distribution models can be used as geographic priors to help classify data from camera traps and acoustic recorders. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models by training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also matches or outperforms existing baselines on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.
  </details>

- **[Subspace Crystallization in Grokking: Rank Compression Tracks the Phase Transition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35112)**  `arXiv:2610.35112`  
  _Shlok Mehendale, Paras Chopra_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Grokking describes understanding something deeply and intuitively. In neural networks, it is the phenomenon where a network generalizes long after memorizing its training data. This delay has been linked to a fall in the effective rank of the network's weight matrices, but whether this rank compression drives grokking or follows it is still unresolved. We study a mean-field MLP and a one-layer transformer trained on modular arithmetic and observe that: (i) Compression follows the onset, not memorization. Every transformer memorizes its training data within 250 steps, while the grokking onset (the first step at which test accuracy reaches 95%) varies from 6,500 to 21,000 steps. The steepest fall in effective rank comes about 900 steps after the onset, however late the onset occurs, and networks that memorize without grokking compress far less. (ii) Subspace crystallization. We call the span of the fewest top singular directions of a weight matrix that preserve 99% of test accuracy its sufficient subspace. Its size can shrink as the margin between the correct and the best wrong output grows, so we also count the directions needed to keep the outputs within 10%. In the transformer, this count falls during the transition from a quarter or more of the available directions to about a tenth, which we call subspace crystallization. (iii) Imposing low rank does not speed up grokking. Against a factorized full-rank control, capping the rank of the transformer's MLP input weights delays the onset, and capping the rank of its embedding stops 15 of 20 runs from grokking. Compression is therefore a signature of grokking rather than its cause.
  </details>

- **[PINND: Physics Informed Neural Networks for Solving the Drift-Diffusion Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33133)**  `arXiv:2610.33133`  
  _Luke Ragan, Matteo G. C. Alasio, Enrico Bellotti, Luca Dal Negro_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The drift-diffusion equations are the fundamental building block for the modeling, design, and optimization of modern semiconductor devices. Solutions of the drift-diffusion equations rarely give way to analytical forms, and exhibit strong nonlinearity, with the solutions ranging over several orders of magnitude. These attributes have led to research into numerical solvers, and while many commercial Technology Computer Aided Design (TCAD) packages now exist, they may require long simulation times, exhibit sensitivity to initial guesses, and rely on mesh generation. Further, these solvers are not well suited for inverse problems where the design parameters of a device are retrieved from its desired functional characteristics. To address all these challenges, this work demonstrates the usage of Physics Informed Neural Networks for the Drift-diffusion (PINND) equations with errors comparable to traditional simulation software using advanced training techniques to solve problems beyond the well-behaved equilibrium regime. For this study, we specifically choose an abrupt PN-junction in both one and two dimensions that features extreme gradients of the carrier concentrations at the Ohmic contacts and an abrupt discontinuity in the doping profile. Using the proposed PINN architecture, we are able to retrieve accurate results for all observables under all bias conditions. Additionally, we apply the PINN solver towards the inverse problem of retrieving doping profiles directly from desired electric field distributions or electrostatic potentials under non-zero applied biases. Our work establishes a powerful PINNs-based approach for semiconductor device modeling with the ability to solve inverse problems under non-equilibrium conditions for microelectronics research and discovery.
  </details>

- **[Nominate-then-Adjudicate: LLM-Assisted One-Pass and Per-Instance MIP Solver Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29391)**  `arXiv:2610.29391`  
  _Yifan Zhao, Qianyang Zhao, Xinyu Guan, Kai Wei, Yuming Deng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Parameter configurations control presolving, cut generation and branching strategies in mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers, directly affecting solving efficiency. Effective configurations vary across instances, while searching for them online requires additional solver runs. We propose Nominate-then-Adjudicate: an empirical performance model (EPM) shortlists candidates from a fixed portfolio, and one large language model (LLM) call selects using static features, compressed formulation text and memory distilled from offline solver measurements. Text exposes distinctions omitted by the chosen aggregate features; selection requires no online candidate solves or foundation-model weight updates. Across sixteen synthetic families, adjudication improves on the EPM's top-ranked candidate (top-1), raising mean normalized performance score from 0.377 to 0.426 and the win rate against SCIP's default from 84.9% to 90.2%; all ten sequential batches show positive mean-score gains. On 400 Ecole instances, it outperforms the per-instance baseline ISAC+ in mean runtime-based score, with gains concentrated in facility location. Total solver time falls by 69.6% versus default, excluding LLM latency. Ablations support text and memory; a second LLM improves overthis http URLcode is available at [this URL](this https URL)
  </details>

- **[Global Convergence in Deep Networks via the Second Law of Thermodynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24775)**  `arXiv:2610.24775`  
  _Matan Tsipory, Ofir Gaash, Itamar Harel, Nathan Srebro, Daniel Soudry_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing convergence analyses of finite-width overparameterized deep neural networks under standard parameterization often rely on parameters remaining close to their initialization and typically neglect the role of noise, despite empirical evidence that stochasticity can improve optimization and generalization. To bridge this gap, we study $L_2$-regularized continuous-time Langevin dynamics (CLD) with isotropic noise, for training feedforward networks with smooth activations. We introduce a change-of-measure inequality, inspired by the second law of thermodynamics, that enables control of key properties of the training dynamics under the time-evolving parameter distribution. Leveraging a sharpened lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) at initialization, we show that injected noise helps preserve NTK stability with high probability without confining the weights to a small neighborhood of their initialization. As a result, we derive a non-asymptotic upper bound on the expected training loss. Our analysis yields explicit conditions on width and noise temperature that guarantee convergence to a finite loss floor. Finally, we experimentally show the network Jacobian can change from initialization, departing the commonly analyzed lazy regime.
  </details>

- **[Pairwise AUC Optimization Needs Corrective Power: A Unified View](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21743)**  `arXiv:2610.21743`  
  _Jia Chen, Zhiyong Yang, Shilong Bao, Qianqian Xu, Qingming Huang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Direct pairwise AUC-surrogate training is attractive because it trains toward the ranking metric used at test time, especially under class imbalance. This creates a direct alignment between the training objective and the evaluation metric, but such metric alignment alone does not guarantee that stochastic training remains corrective. We study this gap through Corrective Power: whether pairwise mini-batch updates produce stronger and more reliable improvements for more severe positive-negative ranking errors. Our main observation is that direct pairwise training can enter regions where severe errors remain common but no longer produce useful corrective motion. In such regions, even the mini-batch noise that would normally help SGD move along the steepest severe-error correction direction can become much weaker. In this paper, we seek a theoretical explanation for this by exploring the degenerate property of the U-statistics formed from the pairwise gradients therein. Our results provide a mechanistic explanation for several empirical patterns: (a) squared-hinge loss is often an effective AUC surrogate; (b) cross-entropy warm-up can help models that enter the AUC phase from a poor starting region; and (c) parameter-efficient fine-tuning from a pretrained model can reduce that need by starting closer to a favorable ranking geometry. Experiments on 8 CV tasks and 8 NLP tasks, using ResNet50, DenseNet121, DistilBERT-base, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, support these predictions.
  </details>

- **[Exhaustive Canonical Skeletons Generation: A Formal Dataset for Decomposable Symbolic Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20108)**  `arXiv:2610.20108`  
  _Giorgio Morales, Anikó Ekárt_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Neural symbolic regression (SR) models require diverse datasets of mathematical expressions for robust training. However, existing datasets rely predominantly on stochastic sampling methods, which suffer from high structural redundancy and incomplete functional coverage. To address this, we introduce an exhaustive dataset of univariate canonical skeletons generated via a deterministic constrained context-free grammar. A canonical skeleton acts as a generic structural representation that subsumes more specific functional forms, eliminating redundant expressions and avoiding repeated computational efforts. Although our dataset consists of univariate skeletons, it is designed to support the decomposable SR paradigm to solve multivariate SR problems without assuming linear separability. Furthermore, we pair this dataset with a sampling strategy that generates clean numerical data without triggering numerical instabilities or relying on artificial protected operators. Canonicalizing two existing neural SR datasets reveals that our dataset is substantially more compact, eliminates structural repetitions, and achieves a uniform operator distribution free of simplicity bias. Finally, we establish a benchmark of 150 SR problems across three tiers, on which state-of-the-art SR methods are shown to struggle significantly.
  </details>

- **[Memorization and Malign Generalization in Conditional Diffusion Models with Random Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11288)**  `arXiv:2610.11288`  
  _Gwangho Kim, Sungyoon Lee_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Conditional diffusion models generate diverse, novel, and high-quality samples under prescribed conditions. However, theoretical understanding of their memorization and generalization remains limited, while recent works have characterized these behaviors primarily in unconditional settings. In this work, we analyze a random-feature conditional score model in the high-dimensional proportional limit, deriving asymptotic expressions for training and test losses. By decomposing the test loss, we show that in the overparameterized regime, increasing model width improves prediction of the condition-dependent mean while reducing within-condition prediction variance, a phenomenon we term "malign generalization." We further show that in the infinite-width limit, the model predicts the conditional mean as accurately as ridge regression of the data on the condition, while its within-condition variance vanishes. Finally, analyzing the training loss reveals that more informative conditions lead to memorization of training samples at smaller widths. These theoretical findings are supported by experiments with U-Net architectures on realistic data.
  </details>

- **[Distilling Graph Geometry: Knowledge Gap from GNNs to MLPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.10520)**  `arXiv:2610.10520`  
  _Zhewei Chen, Hao Zhu, Jiaojiao Jiang, Ahad N. Zehmakan_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  GNN-to-MLP distillation aims to retain the predictive accuracy of a message-passing teacher while deploying a graph-free MLP at inference. Existing methods mainly transfer node-wise predictions or use confidence-based reweighting, but they do not specify where the student should preserve the teacher's graph-induced geometry. We show that this omission leads to two spectral failure modes in the student's representation space. On sparse graphs, the student suffers from spectral underfit, missing high-energy teacher directions induced by aggregation. On dense graphs, it suffers from spectral overfit, retaining spurious directions that the teacher has collapsed through aggregation. Motivated by an energy-weighted teacher-student alignment objective, we propose Graph Geometry-aware MLP (G^2MLP), a training-time distillation framework guided by Ollivier-Ricci curvature. Curvature acts as a local proxy for allocating supervision between prediction-level and representation-level alignment. The deployed model is a standard MLP with no graph access at inference. Across node-classification benchmarks, G^2MLP improves over graph-free distillation baselines in most settings, reduces the teacher-student rank gap in both regimes, and transfers to Graph Transformer teachers and link prediction.
  </details>

- **[When Should an In-Context Learner Expand Its Hypothesis Space?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09471)**  `arXiv:2610.09471`  
  _Weihan Li, Xinlei Chen, Junhao Wu, Tianshi Zheng_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Learning systems adapt quickly within a familiar family of models. The harder step is deciding, from a prediction failure, whether opening a richer family is worth its cost. We cast this as a costly sequential decision and introduce the Structural Revision Environment (SRE), which produces matched failures from noise, exceptions, change within the family or structure outside it, varies the price of expansion and the remaining horizon independently of the evidence, and admits an exact normative solution of the one-shot decision. The solution shows that revision is a value boundary, not an evidence threshold: except at the lowest prices, the richer family becomes the more probable explanation long before expanding becomes optimal. Small Transformers trained in SRE reproduce the expansion boundary from utility alone. Pretrained 7B and 8B language models fail at a definite point: their predictions carry a failure-sensitive signal that their decisions do not reflect. Told the gain of expanding, they weigh it against price and horizon only when they reason, and the one model that finishes its reasoning on the history alone still does not estimate that gain. Controlled post-training of the small Transformers moves the prior and the sharpness of predictions, and neither moves the criterion.
  </details>

- **[When the Agent Edits Its Own Limits: Evaluating a Write-Time Floor Against Prompt Prohibitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06274)**  `arXiv:2610.06274`  
  _Sajib Hossain, Moeen Uddin Mahmud_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Many agent runtimes give the agent a tool for editing its own configuration. Some settings grant abilities, such as enabling a tool. Others set the agent's limits: where it may write, who may message it, which address it listens on, how callers authenticate, and the gate that blocks risky writes. We measure how often models widen those limits while handling ordinary requests, and how well two kinds of defence hold: a prohibition in the system prompt, in three wordings, and a check at the point of writing that we call a containment floor. Every case records whether a protected write was attempted and whether it was saved, read from the tool's arguments and from the file rather than from the model's reply. With no defence, a frontier model saved a protected value on 25 of 72 requests, often when the request never named the field. A prompt that listed the protected field names stopped every request that used those names and did not reduce writes on requests that only described the goal; a prompt that described the forbidden effects did the reverse. With the floor, 0 of 167 protected writes were saved while 65 were attempted. A single-pass pilot on two further models shows the same pattern. We draw four lessons for evaluating agent safeguards: count attempts beside outcomes, test a prompt defence with requests written in a different vocabulary from the prompt, check that a zero means the safeguard fired, and log what the harness sends to the model, because a request-ordering defect in our own runtime was invisible in the transcripts and was found again, independently, by a later benchmark.
  </details>

- **[Poisson-GENERIC Neural Operators: Exact Metriplectic Structure in Function Space via Casimir Entropies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05570)**  `arXiv:2610.05570`  
  _Jason Sulskis, Sathya Ravi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Existing thermodynamically consistent neural operators enforce GENERIC degeneracy by projecting the reversible operator, introducing state dependence without guaranteeing Jacobi. We instead use a compatible Lie--Poisson pencil $L=\alpha D+\lambda(uD+Du)$ for nonlinear transport and constant Poisson multipliers otherwise. Augmenting the observed field $u$ with a latent entropy density $s$ makes $S=\int s$ a Casimir, so $L\,\delta S/\delta z=0$ without projection. The energy combines a fixed mechanical quadratic, a learned gauge-free potential, and a convex internal energy; the friction operator $M=AA^\top$ enforces $M\,\delta E/\delta z=0$ pointwise and supports diffusion and damping without a separate transport generator. Skewness, positivity, and both degeneracies hold for any parameters; the continuum pencil satisfies Jacobi, verified on the alias-free band; the closed-form heat and damped-wave friction operators are representable; physical energy is bounded under coercivity assumptions; and a discrete-gradient integrator preserves both laws in discrete time. On four PDEs in 1D and 2D with three backbones (FNO, Transolver, CNO), at equal optimizer steps the model wins 62/72 seed-level comparisons against unconstrained baselines, recovers the exact transport and wave symbols, matches heat and Burgers dissipation within 12\%, and dissipates nothing on advection; at equal wall-clock the unconstrained FNO is the more accurate ten-frame surrogate. What the structure gives at any budget is the energy balance: over a hundred frames, in and out of distribution, the model never raises the physical energy and conserves it where dissipation vanishes, whereas the unconstrained FNO loses a quarter of a conserved energy off distribution and projected GENERIC-FNO creates energy on most frames. Late-time under-damping on heat and explicit-integrator divergence on the wave are reported as limits.
  </details>

- **[Integrated Imputation-Classification for Supervised Learning with Missing Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04273)**  `arXiv:2610.04273`  
  _Yue Liu, Ben Liang, Ali Tizghadam, Ilijc Albanese_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We study supervised classification problems with missing feature values. Existing approaches often decouple imputation from classification, producing imputations that may be plausible but uninformative for prediction. Instead, we propose the Integrated Imputation and Classification Network (IICN), which jointly trains an imputer and an ${(n{+}1)}$-class discriminator adversarially with a single class-supervised objective, where the discriminator learns to distinguish among the $n$ true classes and an additional ``imputed'' class. We prove that it admits a global optimum where the imputer and discriminator together implement marginalization over missing coordinates and yield a Bayes-optimal classifier. We evaluate IICN on FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and tabular datasets with naturally occurring missingness. IICN outperforms classical impute-then-classify pipelines and recent generative baselines, showing strong robustness and accuracy in challenging settings.
  </details>

- **[MLoRA:Continual Low-Rank Adaptation via Relative-Response Subspace Selection and Momentum Orthogonalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02283)**  `arXiv:2610.02283`  
  _Junkang Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) provides a parameter-efficient approach to continual learning, but its nominal rank can conceal a loss of effective adaptation capacity. We identify \emph{spectral plasticity collapse}: during sequential adaptation, update energy becomes concentrated in a small subset of singular modes, leaving much of the available low-rank space underutilized. This exposes a limitation of interference avoidance alone: protecting historical representations does not ensure that the remaining adaptation capacity is responsive to new tasks or effectively utilized. To address this problem, we propose \texttt{MLoRA}, which jointly controls capacity allocation and utilization. First, historical whitening identifies input directions with strong current-task response relative to accumulated historical response, yielding a task-adaptive basis that remains fixed during training. Second, approximate polar orthogonalization of momentum updates reduces spectral concentration within theselected space. An orthonormal basis connects these mechanisms by transferring the factor-update spectrum exactly tothe induced weight update. We establish a max--min characterization of exact subspace selection and derive cumulative spectral bounds under controlled cross-step anisotropy. Across five class-incremental benchmarks and eight incremental settings, \texttt{MuLoRA} achieves the highest mean accuracy in 15 of 16 reported metrics.
  </details>

- **[Why Does Train-Validation Separation Emerge? Update-Pressure Density Dynamics in Pretrained Backbones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01425)**  `arXiv:2610.01425`  
  _Yuchen Li, Zongqi Fan, Ken-Tye Yong, Nguyen H. Tran_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  During fine-tuning, training accuracy often continues to improve after validation accuracy levels off, widening the empirical gap. We propose a support-transfer account: early updates reuse broadly shared structure, while later fitting relies increasingly on narrower structure with less benefit for held-out examples. From fixed training probes, we normalize per-example gradient magnitudes and measure their pooled dispersion, $D_{\mathrm{den}}$, and their probe-count-weighted within-class dispersion, $D_{\mathrm{within}}^{\mathrm{wt}}$. A local model gives conditions for dispersion and directional cross-entropy separation to grow together, separating uniform logit scaling; additional decision-boundary conditions characterize accuracy-gap growth. A controlled five-level hierarchy tests the effect of sample-private support. A 240-branch intervention matrix crosses training-progress anchors, batch sizes, private shares, and gradient-differentiation doses. The negative gap dose response is clearer at later training stages and is retained across the four batch sizes. A further 48 branches replicate its direction across additional seeds at a fixed stage and batch. Both normalized readouts are positively associated with the accuracy gap in all 90 language fine-tuning runs across three backbones and six tasks. The same direction holds in all 20 vision runs across four datasets. Together, the controlled hierarchy, targeted intervention, and real-model trajectories support a connection between evolving gradient differentiation and train-validation separation.
  </details>

- **[One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00518)**  `arXiv:2610.00518`  
  _Zhangyong Liang, Ying Huang, Haibin Ling_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  One-step generative models construct a static generator through iterative training-time transport. Existing transport objectives primarily assess distributional motion, although a neural generator needs to realize the requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates. The training-time construction raises the question: \emph{once training becomes the iterative process that constructs the final one-step map, what to optimize: the next distributional move, or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map?} To address the question, we introduce \textbf{T}raining \textbf{D}ynamics \textbf{A}ction (\textbf{TDAction}), which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining a prescribed level of distributional progress. We formulate the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derive a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch. The criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs; under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation that constructs shared detached targets without adding an inference-time trajectory. Controlled studies examine the relationship between generator geometry, transport selection, and realized local action. On ImageNet $256\times256$, TDAction attains an FID below $1.1$ without distillation.
  </details>

- **[Quantum-Inspired Score-Based Variational Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39164)**  `arXiv:2609.39164`  
  _Yuchen Cong, Zerui Tao, Chao Li, Zhe Sun, Qibin Zhao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Score-based variational inference (SBVI) provides an alternative to classical Kullback--Leibler (KL)-based variational inference by learning a distribution using only score queries of the target. EigenVI~\cite{cai2024eigenvi} formulates SBVI as an eigenvalue problem, but faces two limitations: the number of variational parameters grows exponentially with the data dimension, and the single-eigenvector formulation cannot represent the full minimum-eigenvalue eigenspace. We propose QuanVI, a quantum-inspired SBVI algorithm that addresses both limitations. Rather than selecting a single eigenvector, QuanVI captures a learned subspace through a density-operator formulation. To enable scalable computation, \model{} employs a matrix-product-operator (MPO) structure parameterized by a quantum tensor network (QTN) with unitary-constrained local tensors and auxiliary ancilla wires. Numerical experiments demonstrate the scalability of QuanVI beyond EigenVI and competitive performance on synthetic distributions and Bayesian posterior-approximation benchmarks, including challenging non-Gaussian targets. The code is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[The Vote Hides the Failure: Aggregation Choice and Noise Robustness in Heart Murmur Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37161)**  `arXiv:2609.37161`  
  _Nicholaus Dismas Ladislaus, Olatunji Damilare Emmanuel, Samuel Chol Buol_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Noise robustness in automated phonocardiogram (PCG) murmur detection, and how it is measured, remains underexamined despite growing interest in low-resource screening. We evaluate two independently reimplemented pipelines, Hierarchical Multi-Scale Convolutional Network (HMS-Net)--CNN, and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM)--LSTM, under controlled, multi-severity noise with noise-augmented fine-tuning and held-out generalization testing. Under matched aggregation, the complete BiLSTM pipeline outperforms the complete HMS-Net pipeline across all conditions in accuracy and Weighted Accuracy. A stable aggregate accuracy score can misrepresent what individual predictions show: HMS-Net's native aggregation degrades under salt-and-pepper noise far less than majority-vote (MV) aggregation at the same severity, a gap reflecting window-level disagreement its native rule absorbs, while BiLSTM's MV accuracy rises after noise-augmented training even though its individual predictions do not improve. HMS-Net's training effect is significant under one accuracy metric but not another. Noise-robustness conclusions can depend as much on evaluation choices as on the models themselves.
  </details>

- **[Progressive Memory Transformer: Memory-Aware Attention for Time-Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31351)**  `arXiv:2609.31351`  
  _Tord Sture Stangeland, Andreas Köhler, Steffen Mæland, Adín Ramírez Rivera_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Time-series carry structure simultaneously at multiple scales (fine-grained variation, mid-range motifs, and global properties) and downstream tasks operate at correspondingly different scales. Most existing self-supervised learning approaches supervise representations globally via instance-level contrastive losses and limited temporal neighborhood supervision, but do not explicitly exploit the structural hierarchy. We propose a learning framework that explicitly enforces a structural hierarchy across three scales independently: a local objective for token alignment, a mid-range objective for window-level motifs, and a global objective for sequence-level agreement. Realizing this framework requires the backbone to expose a representation at each scale; we introduce \textbf{Progressive Memory Transformer} (PMT), which augments a transformer with writable, window-aligned memory that exposes the mid-range scale alongside the token and sequence-level representations conventional transformers already provide. Across eight UCR/UEA/UCI classification benchmarks, a cue-retention probe, and forecasting benchmarks, PMT learns representations that probe well at the global, mid-range, and local scales---strong low-label classification (1--5\% labels), competitive forecasting performance across multiple horizons, and quantitative and qualitative evidence that memory states capture mid-range motifs.
  </details>

- **[Temporal Gradient Inversion for Private Trajectory Reconstruction in Embodied Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30258)**  `arXiv:2609.30258`  
  _Sudip Bhujel, Shanghao Shi, Ruiquan Huang, Ning Zhang, Yang Xiao_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Distributed learning in embodied reinforcement-learning agents offers a degree of privacy by retaining raw sensor data on-device and transmitting only policy gradients to the server. Yet temporal structure can amplify this leakage beyond single-frame attacks. We introduce Temporal Reconstruction Attack on Consecutive Encodings (TRACE), an amortized temporal gradient-inversion attack that autoregressively reconstructs the sequence of private observation-action trajectories from per-step policy-learning gradients. The attack exploits two structural signals ignored by prior single-frame methods: (i) cross-time correlation between successive embodied gradients, which we formalize via a conditional mutual-information bound, and (ii) closed-form action recovery from policy-head gradient structure, which we prove exact when standard entropy regularization is sufficiently small. On held-out embodied scenes, TRACE reaches $18.8$ dB PSNR with near-perfect action recovery at $3$-$4.5$ ms per reconstructed frame, dominating the learning-based baseline across all reconstruction metrics and exceeding optimization attacks while running orders of magnitude faster. Further evaluation demonstrates TRACE's broader applicability across recurrent, residual, and compact transformer victim architectures, multi-modal inputs, and larger discrete action spaces. Defense experiments suggest that protecting temporal gradient streams may require sequence-aware privacy mechanisms.
  </details>

- **[Signed Graph Pre-Training and Prompt Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25722)**  `arXiv:2609.25722`  
  _Zihan Mei, Rong Pan, Yuzhou Chen, Yixuan He_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Signed graphs arise in trust--distrust networks, financial correlation systems, biological interaction graphs, and many other domains in which edges can be positive or negative and may also be directed. While signed graph neural networks have improved task-specific learning, graph transfer learning on signed graphs remains underdeveloped. In this paper, we introduce TopoSIGN, a pioneer topology-guided graph pre-training and prompt learning framework for signed graphs. TopoSIGN combines a structural encoder built on the magnetic signed Laplacian with a novel persistent-homology branch that summarizes signed topology through Dowker-complex persistence images. The fused embeddings are then transferred to a prompt learning function. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of TopoSIGN in extracting useful structural information in signed graphs, as well as the adaptability and flexibility of the proposed general framework.
  </details>

- **[Stable Unsupervised Continual Chunking with Sheaf SyncMap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25143)**  `arXiv:2609.25143`  
  _Xueyuan Li, Danilo Vasconcellos Vargas_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Unsupervised Continual chunking is a fundamental problem in machine learning and neuroscience, where the goal is to identify groups of states that frequently co-occur in temporal sequences. A key challenge is to form accurate chunks while maintaining their stability over time. In this work, we propose sheaf regularization to reduce local inconsistencies in Decentralized SyncMap, a self-organizing system, and thereby stabilize its chunking dynamics. We introduce a radial sheaf structure that penalizes distance-dependent radial motion between pairs of variables. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves the highest normalized mutual information (NMI) among the evaluated SyncMap variants on 12 of 18 probabilistic Continual General Chunking Problem (CGCP) graphs with two-state memory and on 17 of 18 graphs with dynamic memory. In the sequential adaptation experiment, Sheaf SyncMap also achieves high NMI after shifts in the input distribution, indicating that it can adapt to new knowledge while avoiding the negative transfer commonly observed in modern machine learning systems such as neural networks.
  </details>

- **[On Emergent Capabilities and Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24504)**  `arXiv:2609.24504`  
  _Luca Zhou, Emanuele Rodolà_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Model merging combines separately fine-tuned checkpoints by arithmetic on their weights, and is now a routine way to assemble capabilities cheaply. We ask what it does to emergent capabilities: behaviors that arise from fine-tuning but were never an explicit training target. Studying two independent testbeds (activation oracles and emergent-misaligned models) across three model families, we find that the answer is threefold. First, merging preserves an emergent capability that both parents carry: merging two misaligned checkpoints retains most of their broad misalignment across the whole mixing range. Second, merging cannot create an emergent capability that is superadditive in its parents: no weighted merge of two single-task oracles reaches the jointly-trained oracle's auditing ability. Third, when only one parent carries the capability, merging dilutes it faster than the trained capability that accompanies it: the gap is significant in most settings.
  </details>

- **[Displacement Geometry Captures Platonic Shared Reality Across Models and Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24209)**  `arXiv:2609.24209`  
  _Chenming Shang, Yujin Tang, Jun Jie Ou Yang, Ruize Xu, Adam Breuer, Nikhil Singh_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) claims that independently trained models converge on a shared statistical model of reality, yet recent work finds that the evidence weakens under some conditions. In this paper, we measure what models share through the directions (displacement vectors) between samples. Under a single orthogonal alignment limited to just rotation and reflection, these displacement vectors are substantially preserved across 44 independently trained vision and language encoders spanning modalities and asymmetric capability pairs, consistent with the PRH. Pointwise similarity, however, is lower. Representations split into a shared semantic component that is linearly aligned across models, and a private component that is not, which we interpret as having model-specific capabilities. We trace this geometry to concept-level structure: within a model, parent concepts are orthogonal to their child variation vectors; across models, concept displacements are parallel. We predict (and experiments confirm) that fine-tuning preserves Pointwise similarity but reduces displacement similarity, and relational distillation does the opposite. Because semantics align linearly but capabilities do not, we propose importing capabilities from one model to another using a single cached forward pass through the source. We call this Shadow Casting. As a proof of concept, our ShadowCLIP instantiation outperforms strong fine-tuned baselines at far less compute. A cache can be released alongside open model weights, letting one model's capabilities be downloaded and imported into other models with frozen backbones.
  </details>

- **[CoRe-MARL: Cooperative Redistribution Under Unknown Dynamics Using Recurrent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18639)**  `arXiv:2609.18639`  
  _Naimur Rahman Chowdhury, Shatabdi Sen Prapti, Md. Salehin Seyam, Limon Bin Hossain_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Emergency management assistance programs, such as relief distribution, are essential for delivering necessary supplies to affected communities. However, these programs operate in a decentralized network of local centers that face uncertain local demand and supply dynamics, resulting in inconsistent avail- ability of local services. Redistribution of supplies among these local centers reduces these imbalances, but the centers often make decisions independently, with limited information and disrupted transportation. This study develops CoRe-MARL, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework, by formulating a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). We treat each center as an agent that learns a redistribution policy to improve the service in the worst-case region and reduce the service gap across regions while protecting network-wide service. We incorporate a recurrent network that captures evolving supply and demand dynamics without direct observation, while multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) enables centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE). We evaluate the framework in a simulated environment with diverse trajectories, where exact dynamics are not observed by actors and the MAPPO critic. We compare the recurrent MAPPO with the recurrent independent PPO (IPPO) and a local only heuristic, and find that MAPPO reduces the service gap across local centers and enhances service for the worst-served center while maintaining competitive network-wide service. The recurrent MAPPO also shows consistent performance across diverse trajectory patterns, demonstrating its ability to adapt to evolving dynamics. The findings demonstrate the capability of cooperative learning for decentralized redistribution and improving equitable service under uncertain and evolving dynamics.
  </details>

- **[Beyond Embedding Transfer: Component Roles in Grokking Transfer and Stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18078)**  `arXiv:2609.18078`  
  _Zeyu Jia_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Warm-start transfer accelerates delayed generalization (grokking) on algorithmic tasks, yet how internal blocks, residual-stream depth, group non-commutativity, and continual optimization govern transferred circuits remains unclear. Across ten scale-matched batteries ($>1{,}800$ trajectories) on abelian $\mathbb{Z}_{113}$ ($L \in \{1,2,3\}$) and non-abelian $S_5$, transferring internal blocks alongside boundary carriers lifts early accuracy by $5.46$ percentage points and cuts validation confirmation latency by $616.7 \pm 129.0$ steps in 1-layer models ($p_{\rm Holm}=0.004$). In 2-layer models, full transfer compresses trigger onset $8.1\times$ ($+704.7 \pm 84.3$ integral units), whereas omitting donor embeddings incurs a $-4{,}475.6 \pm 76.8$-unit interface deficit. On ternary $S_5$ conjugation ($aba^{-1}$), two-token architectures stall in a unary conjugacy-class shortcut ($\mathrm{Cl}(aba^{-1})=\mathrm{Cl}(b)$, $34.48\% \pm 6.19\%$ peak accuracy). Combining three-token causal routing ($[a,b,a]$) with Peter--Weyl width ($d_{\rm model}=256 > \sum_\lambda d_\lambda^2 = 120$) reaches $97.97\% \pm 1.01\%$ ($80.08\% \pm 7.81\%$ at equal $427\text{k}$ parameters) with $3.2\times$ faster onset than scratch. Under continued AdamW optimization, unshielded circuits relapse by $11.85\%\text{--}80.58\%$ drawdown, and depth-$L$ stability follows a graded $(L-1)$-prefix pinning hierarchy ($75.99\% \to 31.26\% \to 0.32\% \to 0.04\%$ drawdown at $L=3$). Finally, \textbf{Closed-Loop Curvature-Anchored Consolidation} ($\eta_k = \eta_0(1 - A_{\rm val}(k))$ with monotonic AMSGrad second moments) holds saturated drawdown to $0.00\%\text{--}0.12\%$ and lifts pre-saturation terminal accuracy by $+1.67\text{--}5.37$ points over fixed-budget micro-stepping ($87.06\% \pm 0.94\%$ vs.\ $81.69\% \pm 0.90\%$ on $S_5$, $p_{\rm Holm}=0.002$).
  </details>

- **[Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06951)**  `arXiv:2609.06951`  
  _Srikanth Malla, Chiho Choi, Joon Hee Choi_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Activation steering promises modular control of language model behavior: a behavior such as politeness corresponds to a direction in a model's activations, and adding that direction while it generates should switch the behavior on and leave everything else alone. It does not. We ask what decides which other behaviors move, and by how much, and find that on average it points to the model rather than the behavior being steered. Steers mostly lower what the unsteered answer shows and raise a set of behaviors the model falls back on (on Qwen2.5-7B, for example, chiefly what the judge scores as refusal, sycophancy, and poeticism).Three results across 24 behaviors and ten instruction-tuned models support this, every effect read off the generated text by a language-model judge rather than off a probe. That readout matters: on Qwen2.5-7B all 24 behaviors are linearly decodable, but only 20 change what the model writes. First, on average, directions carrying no behavioral content, of a real steer's size and layer, move the same behaviors in a similar order as real steers do, clearly on five models, weakly on five. Second, much interference runs one way, so it cannot be an overlap between two directions: steering profanity makes the model toxic, while steering toxicity leaves profanity untouched. Third, with a behavior held out entirely, geometry measured on the others explains little of the interference it takes part in. The one-way structure and the failure of geometry hold on all ten models. - **[TraceML: What Auto-Research Agents Miss in Long-Horizon ML Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26086)**  `arXiv:2608.26086`  
  _Jiarui Yan, Weiwei Sun, Sijie Li, Wenhan Li, Yiming Yang_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Auto-research agents now run machine-learning development unattended for hours, revising data pipelines, models, and validation from their own feedback, yet on most competitions they still finish below strong human competitors. Outcome-based benchmarks record this gap but not its cause, because they grade the final submission and discard the development process behind it. We introduce TraceML, which pairs human and agent work on the same competitions under one version-level schema: 4,465 human Kaggle trajectories across 134 competitions, seven of which are also worked by two agent scaffolds, giving 430 paired human and 207 agent trajectories. Experts alternate data work, validation, model changes, and ensembling, and return to approaches they had set aside. Each agent scaffold instead collapses into a narrow loop: Codex spends its steps re-weighting ensembles and tuning submissions, MLEvolve mutates its model in place, and neither pivots at the human rate nor reopens abandoned work. A short planning prompt distilled from human practice moves the behaviors it names toward the human profile and lifts scores, but the effort profile stays agent-shaped: instruction closes only the part of the gap that reduces to instructions.   </details>

  _Md Asaduzzaman Jabin, Khoa Le, Lin Zhao, Tianming Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In contrast, current multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based medical AI agents largely operate as stateless inference systems, generating decisions independently for each interaction without retaining or internalizing experiential knowledge. This discrepancy limits their ability to progressively improve reasoning reliability through usage and adapt to longitudinal patient contexts in real-world clinical workflows.   </details>

Across diverse floorplans, RayNO outperforms image-to-image baselines, wireless learning models, monolithic neural operators, and classical multi-fidelity regression on both image-quality and wireless deployment metrics, while reducing the cost of a high-fidelity map from roughly 28 s to 0.11 s.
  </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful approach for improving reasoning in language and vision-language models, yet its strongest successes still depend heavily on ground-truth supervision (e.g., verifiable reward). However, training solely on self-generated feedback can reinforce existing biases, reduce response diversity, and ultimately lead to homogenized responses and training collapse. In this work, we show that unsupervised reasoning can emerge through cooperative multi-agent training. We further show that increasing cohort diversity, through heterogeneous model families, sizes, and rephrased training samples, reduces the correlated errors that drive self-reinforcing feedback loops. This diversity consistently improves reasoning performance and mitigates training collapse. Without any ground-truth labels, Co-RL improves the base models by 3.0-7.9% on average across seven benchmarks and by 1.6-4.4% across four multimodal benchmarks. With learning rate and step budget matched, the two reach held-out accuracies within 0.03 of each other. At higher rates, GRPO falls below its start while SFT does not.   <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

I compare four architectural configurations by selectively removing the attention residual connection, the feed-forward residual connection, or both. At 10M scale, a controlled 8-seed deterministic sweep shows a clear asymmetry: removing the attention residual (FFNOnly) reaches the No-Residual collapse regime (3.350 +/- 0.002), whereas removing the feed-forward residual (AttnOnly) remains well separated from it (1.580 +/- 0.003). During the investigation, I identified and corrected an experimental measurement confound in runtime gain scaling and retained an intermediate reproduction failure rather than excluding it.   <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) handles such budgets using Lagrangian multipliers updated across episodes or Lyapunov virtual queues updated per slot, but their relative behavior under coupled two-sided constraints remains unclear. We formulate this problem and introduce a windowed proportional-fairness objective that captures the temporal distribution of service beyond the classical horizon-average formulation. We characterize the distinct budget-regulation timescales of the two mechanisms through complementary theoretical bounds and identify queue-price buildup as a key mechanism governing finite-horizon budget pacing. Using a common heterogeneous MARL architecture, we compare three utility surrogates and both constraint-handling mechanisms. The results show that utility design primarily determines throughput and fairness, whereas constraint-price dynamics govern training efficiency and budget pacing. Under the default setting, the queue-based PF policy reaches near-final performance after a single training episode, but its unscaled penalty can lead to delayed pacing under tight budgets. Guided by the analysis, we show that queue-price calibration reduces the empirical drift constant by an order of magnitude and substantially narrows the performance gap to Lagrangian methods, which adapt constraint prices across episodes at higher training cost.   </details>

  _Lee Cheuk-Kit, Florentin Coeurdoux, Yuyuan Chen, Sophia Tang, Peter Potaptchik, Yilun Du, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We propose an instantiation of flow matching that relies on a time-independent velocity field---an autonomous flow---to exactly map between two distributions when the target is supported on a sufficiently lower-dimensional data manifold. We also show that the associated one-step generative map is constant in the direction of the autonomous velocity field and therefore satisfies a simple conservation equation, which motivates learning the map directly from samples. These autonomous flows and maps give a dynamical meaning to the flux constraint of Beckmann's transportation problem, and we show that, under suitable conditions, the construction extends beyond flow matching to other probability fluxes satisfying the same constraint. The resulting framework includes, for instance, a closed-form Coulomb transport closely related to Poisson Flow and a flow-matching-consistent version of Equilibrium Matching.   </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A systematic study reveals that the dominant source of degradation in FP4 RL is not training-side quantization error but rollout activation quantization: outliers stretch the dynamic range so far that a large number of activation values underflow to zero under FP4. Counterintuitively, restoring the training policy to higher precision while keeping the rollout in FP4 makes accuracy worse than full FP4 baseline, exposing rollout--training mismatch as the principal failure mode and ruling out standard pretraining-style fixes. We address this with Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ): a single residual correction term constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern, added only to the FP4 rollout matmul -- a lightweight correction that recovers most of the precision lost to outlier-driven underflow without inflating the rollout's compute footprint.   </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have emerged as general-purpose models for time series analysis, but pretraining alone is often insufficient for reliable downstream deployment. Bridging this gap requires further intervention to handle domain shift, task heterogeneity, limited supervision, and computational constraints, which motivates post-training as a broad class of methods to adapt, augment, compose, calibrate, or specialize pretrained TSFMs for downstream tasks. In this work, we analyze TSFM post-training methods based on their locus of intervention in the prediction pipeline, yielding five categories: parameter adaptation, context augmentation, model composition, output processing and uncertainty control, and compression and specialization. Within each category, we study main representative methods and discuss their current limitations. We further identify future directions toward controlled adaptation, reliable context construction, uncertainty-aware model composition, calibrated output processing, and deployment-aware specialization. Overall, by providing a unifying framework for the emerging TSFM post-training landscape, this work aims to support future research to navigate the design space between a pretrained TSFM and its reliable downstream deployment.
  </details>

  _Rahil Sharma_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Before any model comparison, we identify and remove a simulator-specific balance shortcut that would otherwise inflate baseline performance. After this correction, neither the graph features nor the anomaly signal improves Average Precision on the full test set. Both, however, rank fraud better within the subset of cases receiving intermediate baseline scores. In a controlled experiment with injected multi-account fraud rings, engineered structural features recover all injected test transactions, while the tabular baseline misses roughly a quarter of them.   _Runlong Liao, Baiyu Su, Lizhang Chen, Qiang Liu_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  We introduce Signed Rectified Flow (Signed RF), a generalization of Rectified Flow that targets the signed measure $\pi^{sign} = (1+\alpha)\pi^+ - \alpha\pi^-$, where $\alpha>0$, $\pi^+$ is the distribution to promote, and $\pi^-$ is the distribution to suppress. Although direct sampling from a signed measure is not well-defined, Signed RF induces a valid generative process that concentrates probability in regions where the signed measure is positive while provably excluding regions dominated by its negative component. It therefore provides a principled framework for incorporating negative information and exclusion constraints into generative modeling. We analyze the signed continuity equation underlying Signed RF and use a charged-particle interpretation to explain how negative mass forms exclusion barriers. Across several applications, Signed RF improves the fidelity-diversity trade-off on ImageNet, reduces nearest-neighbor similarity in anti-memorization experiments, and reduces nudity induced by adversarial prompts in Stable Diffusion 3.5 while preserving CLIP and aesthetic scores.
  </details>

  _Jakub Paplhám, Willem Waegeman, Eyke Hüllermeier, Vojtěch Franc_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, active learning and selective prediction. However, common epistemic uncertainty scores, such as mutual information or the variance of the predictions, estimate the regret, the excess error of a predictor over the Bayes-optimal predictor. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, and compare this evaluation with the other tasks. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with repeated human labels reveals that the tasks rank the methods differently, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on another. The disagreement is present already at the optimum, where each task calls for a different score. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove that the optimal score is a convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, so that selective prediction and the regret task are the two endpoints of one family of tasks. Out-of-distribution detection, active learning and the regret task thus disagree, theoretically as well as empirically, on which method is a good estimator of epistemic uncertainty, while selective prediction departs from the regret task where the true risk and the regret order the inputs differently. Researchers must therefore state the downstream decision that an epistemic uncertainty estimate is meant to support, instead of relying on a general notion of model ignorance.
  </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Rather than requiring the encoder to capture fine-grained geometry, SinAE shifts the reconstruction burden into an iterative flow-matching decoder, achieving near-lossless reconstruction across domains and reducing reconstruction errors by orders of magnitude relative to prior latent baselines.   </details>

- **[LiteTopK: Exploiting the Curse of Dimensionality for a Fused Indexer-TopK Kernel in Long-Context Sparse Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11976)**  `arXiv:2607.11976`  
  _Ziqi Yin, Jianyang Gao, Peiqi Yin, Jiangneng Li, Gao Cong_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Indexer-TopK, which computes scores and selects the top-$k$ candidates, is a key primitive in long-context sparse attention for large language models, vector retrieval for recommendation systems, and vector databases. However, existing GPU-based Indexer-TopK kernels like DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) typically separate scoring from selection and materialize the full score matrix in high-bandwidth memory. This strategy is inefficient for large score matrices, such as those encountered in long-context sparse attention, due to excessive global-memory traffic, costly synchronization, and prohibitive memory overhead.In this study, motivated by the curse of dimensionality, we observe that sparse attention scores exhibit a score concentration phenomenon, with scores falling within a narrow range. Based on this observation, we propose LiteTopK, a sample-filter-select framework that estimates query-data score ranges from a small subset of the data. It uses these estimates to filter scores as they are computed, materializes only the candidates that pass the filter, and selects from the surviving candidates. In particular, we develop two implementations of LiteTopK. The first uses a conservative threshold estimate, while the second pairs a predicted threshold with a fallback strategy. Building on LiteTopK, we further propose LiteDSA, which reuses overlapping key/value entries across neighboring queries to accelerate attention computation. We integrate LiteTopK into vLLM, SGLang, and Megatron-LM. Our evaluation on eight B200 GPUs demonstrates prefill speedups of up to 1.49$\times$ across GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and Hy-4-Preview at a context length of 1M tokens, without compromising model capabilities.

- **[Prompt Driven Exploration: Language as an Exploration Space for VLA Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08837)**  `arXiv:2607.08837`  
  _Sunshine Jiang, John Marangola, David Zhang, Raghuram Kowdeed, Ruiyang Luo, Nitish Dashora, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Exploration is essential to reinforcement learning (RL) since a policy cannot improve by repeatedly sampling the behaviors it already prefers. Standard methods inject stochasticity in the action space, but such jitter only yields rollouts close to the original action distribution. Escaping a weak policy often requires global perturbations that action noise cannot produce. Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a pathway: they condition the policy on a natural language prompt, and since the rollout follows from it, modifying the prompt induces global changes. The challenge is finding prompts that induce useful global changes. With a weak policy that rarely succeeds, reward is too sparse to select on. Our idea is to refine prompts from the rollouts themselves: a vision-language model (VLM) reasons over the rollout video, diagnoses how the policy responded, and rewrites the prompt to elicit better behavior next time. Sampling a prompt and holding it fixed throughout a rollout provides episode-level commitment, analogous to posterior-sampling exploration. We call this strategy Prompt Driven Exploration (PDE). Across manipulation and reasoning tasks, PDE enables RL to learn successful policies even from zero-reward starts, and improves sample efficiency more broadly. Our website is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the geometry of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_\rho$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and empirically show that harder tasks exhibit greater effective dimension. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and final hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on 86 mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset and three Qwen2.5 model scales (0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B), $d_\rho$ achieves difficulty-prediction AUROC of $0.90$, $0.94$, and $0.96$, respectively. Seven kinematic and positional features predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens, with AUROC between $0.77$ and $0.88$ across scales. These correctness signatures transfer across held-out questions, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.
  </details>

- **[Seahorse: A Unified Benchmarking Framework for Spatiotemporal Event Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01022)**  `arXiv:2607.01022`  
  _Yahya Aalaila, Sebastian Vollmer, Gerrit Großmann_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Spatiotemporal point processes (STPPs) model event data in continuous time and space, with applications in mobility, epidemiology, and public safety. Recent neural STPPs span expressive intensities, density models, continuous-time latent dynamics, normalizing-flow spatial decoders, and score-based generative mechanisms. Yet comparison remains fragile because implementations differ in preprocessing, coordinate normalization, splits, likelihood conventions, and evaluation protocols. We present Seahorse, a unified framework for reproducible training and evaluation of STPPs. Seahorse provides an encode-evolve-decode interface and an executable benchmarking contract that standardizes dataset handling, tuning, raw-coordinate likelihood reporting, and run artifacts across classical baselines, neural likelihood models, continuous-time Neural STPP variants, and sample-based generative models. On 13 real datasets and 19 presets, no model dominates: likelihood, calibration, and next-event prediction favor different models, and the strongest models take from minutes to hours to train. Using HawkesNest as a controlled synthetic stress-test suite, we show how diagnostic benchmarking can probe neural STPP behavior under increasing spatiotemporal entanglement. Seahorse provides reusable infrastructure for comparing, diagnosing, and extending STPP models beyond implementation-specific leaderboards. The implementation, including preset configurations and reproduction scripts, is available atthis https URL.
  </details>

- **[Muon learns balanced solutions in matrix factorization without slow saddle-to-saddle dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30509)**  `arXiv:2606.30509`  
  _Mark Rhee, Jamie Simon, Dhruva Karkada_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Matrix factorization (i.e., problems of the form $\min_{\mathbf{P},\mathbf{Q}} \|\mathbf{M}^\star - \mathbf{P}^\top\mathbf{Q}\|_\mathrm{F}^2$) is a minimal learning problem that exhibits both nonlinear parameter dynamics and representation learning. In this setting, we study how parameter trajectories under the Muon optimizer differ from those of gradient descent. We identify three main dynamical differences: (1) Muon avoids the slow saddle-to-saddle dynamics of GD from small initialization. Muon instead learns all the top singular vectors of $\mathbf{M}^\star$ at the same rate, and they saturate in order of increasing (rather than decreasing) singular value. (2) Muon does not diverge even when the learning rate exceeds the critical threshold set by the local loss sharpness. This frees the learning rate from the condition number of the problem, enabling rapid convergence via exponential learning rate annealing. (3) Once the weights are aligned with each other and the target, Muon flow conserves the matrix quantity $\sqrt{\mathbf{P}^\top \mathbf{P}}-\sqrt{\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{Q}}$, while gradient flow is known to conserve the matrix $\mathbf{P}^\top\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{Q}$. Despite having distinct conserved quantities, both optimizers find the so-called balanced solution from vanishing initialization. When training from small random initialization, the weights spontaneously align early in training. We derive the alignment rates in simple settings and show that they predict the empirical alignment rates in general. Finally, we exploit structural properties of Muon to construct a learning rate schedule that achieves near-perfect alignment in only two optimization steps.
  </details>

- **[USAD: Uncertainty-aware Statistical Adversarial Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27832)**  `arXiv:2606.27832`  
  _Zhijian Zhou, Xunye Tian, Jiacheng Zhang, Zesheng Ye, Yiyi Guo, Donghao Zhang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Statistical adversarial detection (SAD) treats detection as a two-sample test. Given a reference set of clean examples (CEs) and a batch of queries, potentially containing an unknown mixture of CEs and adversarial examples (AEs), SAD decides whether the query distribution drifts away from the CE distribution while controlling the false-alarm rate. Existing SAD-based methods mainly use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to measure the distributional discrepancy. However, MMD's distributional properties limit its ability to capture characteristic uncertainty patterns of AEs that are crucial for detection: AEs typically exhibit abnormal feature spread (i.e., global uncertainty) and instability under perturbations (i.e., local uncertainty). To close the gap, we propose Uncertainty-aware Statistical Adversarial Detection (USAD), which explicitly captures these uncertainty patterns with two new statistics: (1) Variance Discrepancy (VD), which measures the difference in feature spread between AEs and CEs to capture global uncertainty differences. (2) Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD), which compares feature covariance under Gaussian perturbations to capture local uncertainty differences. By aggregating VD and PCD, USAD achieves superior detection performances over baseline methods against various adversarial attacks, highlighting the importance of considering characteristic behaviors of AEs for effective SAD. Our code is available at:this https URL.
  </details>

- **[SOAP-Bubbles $\circ$\ding{109} Structured Weight Uncertainty for Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23357)**  `arXiv:2606.23357`  
  _Adrian Robert Minut, Nico Daheim, Marco Miani, Mohammad Emtiyaz Khan, Wu Lin, Thomas Möllenhoff_
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  Structured weight-uncertainty can improve many aspects of deep learning, but it remains costly to estimate and difficult to implement. Here, we show that these issues can be addressed by adapting the SOAP optimizer. Our key idea is to run IVON, an existing diagonal-covariance variational method, in the eigenspace of SOAP's preconditioner and then use the preconditioner to transform the diagonal estimate into a non-diagonal covariance. The resulting method has costs similar to those of SOAP and requires no drastic changes to training pipelines. We call the posteriors obtained in this way SOAP-Bubbles and our new optimizer Eigenspace-VON (EVON). We show that, for logistic regression, EVON can match the full Gaussian covariance and that, for language model pretraining, it yields significantly better results than existing diagonal-covariance methods. Our work makes it easier to estimate more expressive posterior distributions for deep learning at scale.
  </details>

- **[Demystifying Numerical Instability in LLM Inference: Achieving Reproducible Inference for Mission-Critical Tasks with HEAL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21023)**  `arXiv:2606.21023`  
  _Zhenting Zhu, Lucas Thai, Shan Yu, Yicheng Liu, Yifan Qiao, Chenxi Wang, et al._
  <details><summary>Abstract</summary>
  As Large Language Models (LLMs) deploy into mission-critical domains (e.g., finance, medicine, and law), output reproducibility has become a strict system requirement.
